2 Data cleaning

Every row removal is a rule, and the audit reconciles exactly.

Stage Rows
Raw rows 541910
Missing CustomerID (dropped) 135080
Missing Description (dropped) 1454
Cancellations (dropped) 8905
Non-positive UnitPrice (dropped) 40
Quantity outliers (invoice dropped) 779
Final rows 397106

Four rules, in order: drop rows with no CustomerID; drop rows with no Description; drop cancellations (quantity or price <= 0, or a C-prefixed invoice number); drop the entire invoice containing a quantity outlier above a Tukey outer fence. Dropping only the negative leg of a cancelled order would leave the original in place.

3 Segments

Segment 1 is always the lowest-value group by construction — k-means returns clusters in arbitrary order, so labels are remapped by ascending median spend. Without that, any statement of the form “cluster 3 is the most valuable” would be unfalsifiable.

5 Validation

between_SS/total_SS is an in-sample statistic: it measures how well k-means fit the data it was given, and it is monotone in k, so it cannot validate anything. These are the out-of-sample diagnostics.

6 Customer retention and CLV

CLV is expected future activity x observed purchase rate x average order value x assumed margin. Every factor is either directly observed or comes from a fitted curve:

  • purchase rate — orders per week of observed active lifetime (first purchase to last purchase), not per week of calendar tenure.
  • remaining life — the Kaplan-Meier curve, conditioned on the customer having survived to their current age: int_a^{a+H} S(u) du / S(a).
  • churn — a customer whose last purchase is older than the censoring window has already churned and is worth zero.
Retention: the Kaplan-Meier model used for CLV, and a rejected parametric fit.

6.1 The Weibull fit was rejected

The dashed line above is a Weibull maximum-likelihood fit, computed and then discarded. It disagrees with the non-parametric estimate by a mean absolute 0.31 in survival probability, predicting 7% still active where Kaplan-Meier says 50%.

Retention here drops steeply and then flattens — a mixture of customers who churn almost immediately plus a long-lived tail. No single Weibull can represent that shape, so CLV uses the Kaplan-Meier curve, which assumes nothing about the form of the lifetime distribution. BG/NBD was implemented first and abandoned for the same reason: its likelihood failed to reproduce a Monte Carlo simulation of its own generative process. Reasoning for both is in R/05_clv.R.

Single-purchase customers are excluded from the lifetime fit: their first and last purchase are the same day, so they have no measurable duration.

Segment profiles. A churned customer (last purchase older than the censoring window) has a predicted CLV of zero by construction, which is why the dormant segment’s median is £0.

7 Where the value sits

Revenue by country, UK excluded. The UK dominates total revenue.
Revenue and orders by month; the November-December gift season dominates the year.

Revenue is highly seasonal and domestic. Segment 2 is 39.5% of customers but 86% of revenue; the dormant segment has a median predicted CLV of zero.

8 Limitations

  1. The gross margin is assumed, not measured. The dataset has revenue only. Every CLV figure scales linearly with it.
  2. CLV is not validated against outcomes. The dataset ends, so there is no holdout period to check predictions against realised spend. This is the first item in the README’s “what I’d do next”.
  3. k=2 is coarse. The elbow method prefers k=4, which gives four clean tiers. k=2 ships because that is what the silhouette supports.
  4. The wholesale channel is largely absent. Customers with no CustomerID were dropped from customer-level segmentation; they carry ~17% of revenue and include bulk trade accounts, so “Champions” describes registered retail buyers only.
  5. Single-purchase customers have no measurable lifetime, so the retention curve is estimated from repeat customers only (66% of the base).
